guides.title: Resolve a session before checking roles
guides.summary: Use application-owned session validation to populate the trusted request user, then apply role or permission middleware.
guides.markdown:
Authentication resolves a trusted user from a session. Authorization decides which operations that user can perform. createAuth accepts extractSessionId, validateSessionId and resolveUserById callbacks. The application owns session storage and user lookup. createSessionManager can supply expiry, rotation, revocation and cookie policy behind typed storage callbacks. Use an opaque session token and trusted server storage. A claimed user ID, role or permission from the browser is not authentication.

Run auth.middleware before authorization guards. It populates context.get('user') after session and user validation. Missing or invalid sessions stay anonymous. Provider failures also stay anonymous. createAuthorizer builds middleware around application hasRole and hasPermission callbacks. Missing callbacks deny the corresponding checks. requireRole accepts any listed role. requireAllRoles requires every listed role. Anonymous denials use 401 and authenticated permission denials use 403 by default.

Install the middleware in the framework application or relevant page/layout guards. Transport guards use the transport request. Apply resource authorization per action for record access. A WebSocket connection guard does not recheck each later message. Native entrypoints must parse and authorize explicitly.

createLoginHandler accepts credential validation and an application session creator. The provider can also supply createSession for reuse. Set cookie attributes and merge returned headers into the actual response. Define logout, expiry and session rotation in the application. OAuth setup requires provider credentials and callback handling. This example does not create a login route or issue a cookie.

The package currently ships TypeScript source through its main entry. Use the framework Vite pipeline or a compatible TypeScript loader. File presence and static signatures do not prove execution in plain Node. The executable example uses fixed in-memory session fixtures to test middleware ordering and role decisions. These fixture tokens are not production credentials or a persistent session implementation.

guides.title: Authorize a specific server record
guides.summary: Define typed actions against trusted user and record data. Keep permission presentation separate from server enforcement.
guides.markdown:
createResourcePolicy<Resource, User>() accepts named boolean decision callbacks. It retains the action names and application types. Policies read the user from trusted server request context. The application supplies record lookup and persistence. Browser state and resource IDs remain untrusted input.

Use can for a boolean decision and authorize to enforce access. authorize returns the accepted record or throws ResourceAuthorizationError. Anonymous denials have COSSACK_AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED and status 401. Authenticated denials have COSSACK_AUTH_FORBIDDEN and status 403. Missing records are denied. Callback exceptions are internal failures, not deliberate denials.

permissions returns frozen booleans for presentation. Recheck authorization on the server before mutation even when the UI hides a button. policy.action adapts parsed input and trusted request context to Server authorization metadata. Attach it through @Server({ input: schema, authorize: policy.action(...) }). The lookup receives the owned AbortSignal. Do not derive its actor or tenant from browser fields.

policy.middleware performs request-specific lookup and authorization before an HTTP handler. Direct native method calls do not run RPC metadata. Parse input and call authorize explicitly at native entrypoints. Authorization is a decision at one time. Use a transaction or conditional write that repeats trusted ownership predicates when a record can change.

Pass the signal to lookup I/O and check cancellation before effects. Aborting stops waiting for a policy callback but cannot terminate work that ignores cancellation. Rule maps are fixed after construction. Unknown actions and nonboolean decisions do not authorize access.

The executable example uses local Hono request contexts and fixture records. It proves decisions, frozen presentation permissions and parsed-input action lookup. It does not authenticate a real user, make a network request or write to a database. Run it with the framework pipeline or a compatible TypeScript loader because this package ships source.

guides.title: Handle OAuth failures by code and stage
guides.summary: Use fixed library diagnostics for configuration, state, provider and application mapping failures without exposing callback or credential data.
guides.markdown:
createOAuth supplies signed state and PKCE for cookie-based authorization flows. Use a request-scoped secret resolver when server bindings exist only on the request context. The application owns provider credentials, local account mapping, session creation and an atomic OAuthStateStore. Cookie-based flows require stateStore.create and stateStore.consume. The library stores a provider-scoped state digest with absolute expiry, then consumes the active record before token exchange. Only boolean true allows exchange. A reused, expired or unavailable record returns COSSACK_OAUTH_STATE_UNAVAILABLE. Storage exceptions have state-create or state-consume stages and omit raw values. A failed exchange or mapping does not restore consumed state; start a new authorization flow.

OAuthError exposes code, stage, status and an optional numeric providerStatus. Messages are fixed library text. Errors retain no raw exception, provider response body, authorization code, token or credential. toJSON returns only this diagnostic data. Configuration failures throw synchronously when the kit or route is constructed. Redirect preparation failures use the default diagnostic response.

Callback onError receives an immutable OAuthError. Return a Response to control the failure response. Returning nothing preserves the default response. A throwing onError produces COSSACK_OAUTH_ERROR_HANDLER_FAILED. Log error.toJSON rather than the callback URL, cookie, tokens or request context. Context still contains application request data.

Invalid callback parameters or state produce status 400. Denied consent produces 403. Provider rejection, token exchange and user-info failures produce 502. Configuration, redirect preparation, account mapping and error-handler failures produce 500. Account mapping includes the application onUser callback and any session creation it performs. Failures do not undo application writes or sessions already created.

Configured cookie-based callback handlers clear their matching state cookie on success and failure, including denied consent and missing parameters. Cookie deletion is browser cleanup. The required stateStore supplies atomic server-side consumption before token exchange. Provider authorization codes must still be single-use. The shared session manager owns expiry and rotation policy behind application storage callbacks; stronger account consistency and transport freshness remain application-owned. Stateless mode requires application CSRF and replay protection and does not use the state cookie or PKCE verifier.

The example invokes only denied and malformed callbacks. It uses fixture configuration and does not contact a provider, exchange a code or create a session. TypeScript source needs a compatible loader or bundler.

The example uses local memory to keep the failure fixture offline. It does not establish durable or cross-Worker atomicity. Generated applications use one conditional SQL DELETE against purpose-tagged state records. Server state contains no authorization codes, PKCE verifiers or provider credentials. Expired abandoned records require application cleanup.

guides.title: Compose credentials and persistent session storage
guides.summary: Use typed password verification, conditional credential upgrades and explicit session expiry and rotation with application-owned storage.
guides.markdown:
createPasswordHasher uses Web Crypto PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a random 16-byte salt, a 32-byte digest and an encoded work factor. hashPassword and verifyPassword use 100000 iterations and accept at most 1024 UTF-8 password bytes. They do not normalize or truncate passwords. Malformed records and factors above maxIterations are rejected before derivation. The old pbkdf2$salt$digest format is not accepted. Existing accounts need an explicit application migration or password reset. Password policy remains application-owned.

The default preserves the generated Workers setting. Cloudflare's workerd default cap is currently 100000; its local simulator does not enforce that cap. This is below OWASP's 600000 PBKDF2-SHA256 guidance. A successful local test does not prove deployment resource limits. Verify runtime limits before raising iterations, or supply a PasswordHasher implementation with hash and verify. Source: https://github.com/cloudflare/workerd/blob/main/src/workerd/io/limit-enforcer.h and https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html.

createCredentialVerifier infers the account record and safe user from application find, passwordHash and user callbacks. A missing account, missing hash or failed verification returns null. Only boolean true grants verification. The library maps the user only after success. An optional replacePasswordHash callback atomically compares the expected stored hash before writing an upgraded one. False rejects a stale login. Higher accepted work factors are never downgraded. User models, identifier normalization, role lookup and writes stay in the application.

createSessionManager owns opaque random tokens, numeric Unix-millisecond timestamps, absolute expiry and matching cookie headers. AuthSessionRecord has kind auth. AuthSessionStore owns create, read, replace and revoke. Store create must insert without overwriting collisions. Store read must return only auth records. Reset tokens must not be interpreted as auth sessions. Default cookies use session_id, Path=/, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax. Apply returned headers to the response only after the operation succeeds. Do not serialize them or session tokens into page state.

Validation never refreshes expiry. Exact expiry is rejected. Rotation requires one atomic conditional replacement of the expected active record; a read followed by delete and insert is insufficient. Exactly one concurrent replacement may win. Revocation must target auth records. The generated application uses one conditional SQL UPDATE for replacement and preserves account identity and request metadata. The caller owns stronger store guarantees and context scoping. Storage errors and already-expired completions issue no cookie; errors do not undo committed storage effects.

AuthError exposes a fixed code, stage and message without raw crypto or storage exceptions. Use error.toJSON for diagnostics. Persistent validation does not make an existing WebSocket automatically revalidate identity; native session freshness remains a transport policy. OAuth callback replay uses the separate required OAuthStateStore contract, with state-purpose records and atomic consumption before token exchange.

The example uses a local memory store to illustrate the callback contract. It checks verification, exact expiry and concurrent rotation. It does not prove durable or cross-Worker atomicity, native RPC authorization or a production hashing resource budget. TypeScript source needs a compatible loader or bundler.
